talks.title: [WOOT2021] Identifying Valuable Pointers in Heap Data
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for [WOOT2021] Identifying Valuable Pointers in Heap Data.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, James Roney presents research on enhancing memory cartography—a specialized data-oriented attack technique—to identify valuable pointers in heap memory without requiring heap spraying. In a standard memory cartography attack, an attacker with an arbitrary memory read vulnerability navigates through an application's address space along a pre-mapped network of pointers between memory regions (such as static data sections, heaps, and stacks) to leak arbitrary sensitive data without causing segmentation faults. While static data sections maintain deterministic relative layouts despite Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), transitioning from a dynamic, non-deterministic heap allocation to static data sections originally relied on heap spraying predictable objects. Roney and his collaborators introduce a method that uses signature-based byte filtering to reliably identify pointers from uncontrolled heap regions to static data sections.

### Key Topics
- **Data-Oriented Attacks vs. Control-Flow Hijacking**: Unlike traditional control-flow hijacking attacks (e.g., overwriting return addresses) that trigger modern defenses such as stack canaries or Control Flow Integrity (CFI), data-oriented attacks manipulate program variables and data pointers while strictly adhering to legitimate control-flow paths.
- **Memory Cartography Mechanics**: Originally introduced by Rogowski et al., memory cartography creates an offline map of deterministic pointers between memory regions. By chaining these references, an attacker can traverse from an initial leak to target data (such as browser session cookies) across fragmented memory spaces.
- **Heap Non-Determinism Limitation**: Previous memory cartography required spraying known objects into the heap to bridge the gap between dynamic heap memory and static sections. In environments where the attacker cannot control heap allocations, this method fails.
- **Signature-Based Pointer Identification**: An offline analysis technique that characterizes the byte patterns immediately surrounding frequent pointers to static destinations, generating simple byte-level filters that can identify target pointers during runtime heap scanning.

### Technical Details
- **Offline Signature Compilation**: The attacker executes the target application locally multiple times across independent runs with ASLR enabled. By inspecting boundaries (e.g., via Linux `/proc/self/maps`), the attacker tracks heap memory regions and maps all pointers referencing external targets (such as libc or program libraries). The method identifies the most frequently referenced destination offsets across runs. For each target destination, the algorithm inspects a window of bytes surrounding the pointers (preceding bytes, pointer bytes shifting due to ASLR, and trailing bytes) and establishes upper and lower bound value intervals for each position across all runs to construct a byte filter.
- **Online Attack Execution**: At attack time, the attacker scans memory starting from their local heap read vulnerability and evaluates aligned pointer-sized regions against the pre-compiled byte bounds. Once a match is detected, the attacker extracts the pointer to the known static destination, anchoring their memory cartography navigation without crashing the process.
- **Empirical Evaluation**: The approach was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation across 10 memory dumps per target program:
  - *Vim*: Tested as a single-threaded baseline with a unified heap; identified pointers to top frequent destinations with over 99% precision.
  - *Firefox*: Characterized by complex, multi-VMA jemalloc heap chunks. By aggregating relevant jemalloc chunks matching the JavaScript heap, the filter identified pointers to `libxul` with high precision, maintaining strong performance even in the worst-case individual heap chunk.
  - *Apache with OpenSSL 1.0.1 (Heartbleed)*: Evaluated against a real-world read vulnerability scenario, demonstrating equally high precision.

### Takeaways
- **Expanded Threat Surface**: Attackers can reliably locate entry points into static data structures from heap memory using passive signature matching, eliminating the prerequisite of heap spraying.
- **Security Implications**: Highlights the critical need for strict process isolation and independent address spaces for mutually untrusted origins, as in-process mitigations and ASLR do not prevent data-oriented pointer mapping.
- **Assumptions & Future Directions**: The technique relies on stability of inter-region offsets between local analysis environments and victim targets. Future work aims to evaluate complete end-to-end exploits under real-world timing and bandwidth constraints.

talks.title: [DLS2021] 4th Deep Learning And Security Workshop -- Part 1
talks.teaser: Walks through adversarial attacks on antivirus engines, secure federated aggregation, prototype-based training and robocall blocking.
talks.summary:
The opening session of the Deep Learning and Security Workshop 2021 begins with organizer remarks on the year's submissions, then a keynote by Sadia Afroz on attacking commercial malware detectors. Her team modified Windows binaries in the problem space, adding sections, overlay bytes and renamed sections, with reinforcement learning choosing the changes. Adding sections often broke packed malware, so a sandbox check confirmed the functionality was intact and cut broken files to about four percent. Evasion against three commercial antivirus products reached roughly 30 to 50 percent, yet cloud-side detection caught many samples that resembled known malware.

Next, SafeLearn presents secure aggregation for private federated learning. It computes federated averaging with the ABY framework across two non-colluding servers, so only the aggregate is revealed, without a trusted third party. Accuracy matches plain averaging, and server communication for 500 models on a network intrusion task is about 8 megabytes. A prototype-based loss called IUPG treats benign samples as off-target data. On malware classifiers it reduced false negatives and roughly halved false positives on out-of-distribution inputs, and paired with adversarial training it held up best against appended benign content.

The last talk, RoboCallGuard, introduces a virtual assistant that answers unknown calls, asks who the caller wants to reach, and interrupts the caller to separate human telemarketers from robocalls. Against 79 clusters of real robocalls it blocked all of them and labeled about 98 percent correctly, and a 21-person user study found the added delay acceptable. The main limit is targeted calls from callers who already know the callee's name. Practitioners should take away that problem-space attacks and full-pipeline testing reveal more than feature-space or single-vendor evaluations.

talks.title: High-Frequency Trading on Decentralized On-Chain Exchanges
talks.teaser: Shows how transaction ordering lets attackers profitably sandwich traders on automated market makers on decentralized exchanges.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether high-frequency trading works on decentralized exchanges, which settle trades on public blockchains rather than through a central operator, and whether the market can be manipulated to the detriment of traders. Trading volume on these venues has grown sharply over the past year and now rivals large centralized platforms in some comparisons. Miners order pending transactions by publicly known rules, and traders must broadcast their orders over a peer-to-peer network first, so an observer who sees a trade early can insert its own transactions around it.

The focus is on automated market makers that price assets with a constant product formula, where each trade shifts the pool price along a curve. Traders set slippage protection thresholds that revert trades moving too far, and this is what enables sandwich attacks: the attacker trades ahead of a victim to worsen its execution price, then trades back for profit. The researchers derive a minimum profitable victim input, below which no sandwich attack can cover its costs, and propose disabling transactions above that level as a mitigation. Splitting large trades into smaller ones can also help, though it raises fees per transaction. Simulations with several attackers suggest they divide the revenue, and congestion makes break-even harder to reach. A variant where the attacker acts as a liquidity provider is also noted.

The closing point is that transparent blockchain exchanges, combined with the delay before transactions are processed, make market manipulation visible and exploitable. Anyone designing or trading on such venues should account for transaction ordering and slippage settings.

talks.title: Is Private Learning Possible with Instance Encoding?
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Is Private Learning Possible with Instance Encoding?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation examines the viability of achieving privacy-preserving machine learning through instance encoding, focusing on the InstaHide scheme introduced at ICML. Instance encoding adds a pre-processing step where training data is converted into intermediate encodings intended to prevent information leakage while enabling models to train directly on the encoded data. The authors evaluate InstaHide's empirical security by completely breaking its official challenge dataset, present theoretical impossibility results bounding instance encoding privacy when combined with accuracy, and critically assess the role of security challenges in machine learning security research.

### Key Topics
- **Instance Encoding in Machine Learning:** The concept of transforming raw training data into privacy-preserving intermediate encodings that allow downstream algorithms to train without direct access to private samples.
- **InstaHide Architecture:** A mechanism combining linear combinations of private images with samples from an unlabeled public dataset, followed by random pixel sign flipping (masking).
- **Attack on the InstaHide Challenge:** A practical reconstruction attack utilizing neural-network-based clustering followed by image recovery to reconstruct private training images.
- **Theoretical Barriers:** Formal security definitions and impossibility theorems demonstrating fundamental trade-offs between instance encoding accuracy and cryptographic privacy.
- **Evaluation of Security Challenges:** The limitations of relying on static empirical challenges without formal, falsifiable security models and threat definitions.

### Technical Details
- **InstaHide Encoding Mechanism:** InstaHide draws images from both a private labeled dataset and an auxiliary public dataset, creates a linear combination of these images, and applies a masking layer that randomly flips the sign of each pixel with probability 1/2.
- **Challenge Reconstruction Attack:** The InstaHide challenge provided 50 encodings for each of 100 private images using an undisclosed public dataset. The attack operates in two phases: first, a neural network clusters encodings based on the underlying private images they encode; second, an image recovery step reconstructs the original images from each cluster, achieving near-perfect recovery of all 100 challenge images.
- **Alternative Threat Model Attack:** Assuming auxiliary knowledge where the attacker has access to the public dataset used during encoding, the authors developed an efficient attack that scales linearly with data size and reconstructs a private image from just a single encoding.
- **Theoretical Impossibility Bounds:** The authors formulated a security game where an adversary distinguishes which of two identically labeled instances was encoded. They proved that if a protocol achieves accuracy 1/2 + ε on encoded data across two concept functions, a polynomial-time adversary achieves advantage 1/2 + Ω(ε) in breaking privacy. When accuracy is defined on original data, the adversary's advantage is bounded by 1/2 + 1/n (where n is sample complexity), ruling out cryptographic levels of privacy.

### Takeaways
- **InstaHide is Insecure:** InstaHide fails to provide robust privacy, as demonstrated by the complete reconstruction of its official challenge dataset and efficient single-encoding recovery under public dataset knowledge.
- **Fundamental Incompatibility:** Strong cryptographic privacy and high utility/accuracy cannot be achieved simultaneously via instance encoding alone.
- **Challenges Cannot Replace Formal Models:** Security challenges should serve only as necessary conditions for security and cannot substitute for clear threat models and falsifiable claims. The broader machine learning security field must transition from informal evaluations toward rigorous, mathematically defined threat models.

talks.title: MAD-HTLC: Because HTLC is Crazy-Cheap to Attack
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in MAD-HTLC: Because HTLC is Crazy-Cheap to Attack.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Itay Tsabary presents "MAD-HTLC: Because HTLC is Crazy-Cheap to Attack," joint work with Matan Yechieli, Alex Manuskin, and Ittay Eyal. Hash Time Lock Contracts (HTLCs) are standard smart contract primitives fundamental to off-chain scaling solutions like the Lightning Network, atomic swaps, and contingent payments. While previously known to be vulnerable to miner bribery attacks on Ethereum via complex smart contracts, this research demonstrates that bribery attacks against HTLCs are simpler, cheaper, and directly applicable to Bitcoin via standard transaction fees. To resolve this vulnerability systematically, the authors propose MAD-HTLC, an incentive-compatible replacement based on the game-theoretic principle of Mutually Assured Destruction.

### Key Topics
- **HTLC Miner Bribery Vulnerability:** HTLC security relies on the assumption that a valid preimage transaction published before timeout $T$ will be confirmed. However, this ignores miner extractable value (MEV). A sender (Batman) can bribe miners with higher transaction fees to delay the recipient's (Antman's) transaction until the timeout elapses, stealing the locked funds.
- **Subgame Perfect Equilibrium (SPE) Analysis:** Using backward induction to model the game across rounds, the authors prove that when all miners are rational, attack bribery costs are independent of the timeout duration $T$, invalidating the assumption that longer timeouts mitigate attacks.
- **MAD-HTLC Architecture:** A protocol leveraging miner incentives as deterrence. If both parties' preimages are exposed, any miner can claim the entire locked balance as MEV, ensuring both parties lose if an attack is attempted.
- **Bitcoin MEV Feasibility:** Demonstrating through Bitcoin Core patches that implementing MEV and bribery logic requires minimal code and is practical today.

### Technical Details
- **Cost & Empirical Findings:** Analysis revealed Bitcoin HTLCs securing over $26,000 where an attacker could pull off the bribery attack for a cost of merely $2. If the honest party attempts a counter-bribe bidding war, they require a linear fee of roughly 1% of the locked value (e.g., $260 on a $26,000 balance, which is 10,000 times higher than typical transaction fees).
- **MAD-HTLC Design:** Built using two subcontracts (split for Bitcoin Script, consolidatable in Ethereum Solidity):
  1. *Deposit Contract:* Redeemed by Antman presenting preimage 1, by Batman after timeout $T$ presenting preimage 2, or by *any miner* presenting both preimage 1 and preimage 2.
  2. *Collateral Contract (Optional):* Prevents a spiteful Batman from releasing preimage 2 after Antman claims the deposit; Batman reclaims it after timeout $T$, unless both preimages are revealed, in which case miners take the collateral.
- **Security & Incentive Proofs:** Formally modeled using an ideal functionality $\mathcal{F}$ and real hybrid protocol $\Pi$ using universal composability principles, proving indistinguishability alongside SPE game analysis.
- **Overhead & Mainnet Evaluation:** The Bitcoin Script implementation adds an overhead of only a few dollars. Ethereum Solidity has an overhead of roughly $150, reducible to ~$10 when amortized. Deployments on mainnets showed Ethereum transactions were front-run (MEV active), while Bitcoin transactions confirmed smoothly without MEV interference.
- **Bitcoin Core Patches:** To show MEV feasibility on Bitcoin, authors patched Bitcoin Core with a 150-LOC patch to coordinate bribe recognition and transaction delaying, and a 350-LOC patch establishing an external Python RPC infrastructure for custom MEV logic.

### Takeaways
Increasing HTLC timeouts does not protect against rational miner bribery, and relying on the current immaturity of Bitcoin MEV is dangerous. MAD-HTLC provides a practical, drop-in replacement that aligns miner incentives to guarantee protocol execution with negligible fee overhead.

talks.title: The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researcher Jorge Toro presents collaborative research conducted with David Basin and Ralph Sasse at ETH Zurich analyzing the EMV standard (commonly known as chip and PIN). With over 9 billion EMV smart cards in circulation worldwide, the standard is intended to safeguard high-value purchases through PIN verification known only to the legitimate cardholder. Using formal methods, the researchers developed the first comprehensive model of EMV to discover existing and new security issues, notably identifying and practically demonstrating a critical PIN bypass vulnerability in contactless Visa transactions, followed by proposing machine-checked fixes.

### Key Topics
- **EMV Protocol Architecture:** The breakdown of EMV transactions into four core phases: initial application selection and data exchange, offline data authentication (via SDA, DDA, or CDA), cardholder verification methods (offline PIN, online PIN, or Consumer Device Cardholder Verification Method / CDCVM), and transaction authorization (offline terminal acceptance or online issuer authorization).
- **Formal Verification with Tamarin:** Modeling protocol execution paths using multiset rewriting rules and verifying security properties expressed in first-order logic formulas, such as 'bank accepts', 'authentication to the terminal', and 'authentication to the bank' (formalized via injective agreement).
- **Contact EMV Findings:** Confirmation that only transactions combining Combined Dynamic Data Authentication (CDA) with online PIN or no PIN are secure, whereas transactions relying on offline PIN remain susceptible to PIN bypass attacks previously reported in 2010.
- **Contactless EMV & Visa PIN Bypass:** Uncovering that common MasterCard contactless transactions are secure, while common Visa transactions omit cryptographic signatures on Card Transaction Qualifiers (CTQ), allowing an attacker to tamper with the cardholder verification method.

### Technical Details
In the Visa contactless protocol, the card specifies its preferred Cardholder Verification Method (CVM) inside a data object known as Card Transaction Qualifiers (CTQ). Although the specification supports signing the CTQ using Signed Dynamic Authentication Data (SDAD), standard Visa transactions do not mandate or verify this signature. As a result, the CTQ lacks integrity protection.

The researchers weaponized this flaw by constructing an Android application operating a man-in-the-middle attack over a relay architecture. During a high-value purchase where the terminal requests cardholder verification, a genuine card responds indicating that an online PIN is required. The attacker intercepts and modifies the CTQ to indicate that cardholder verification was performed on a consumer device (CDCVM, typical for smartphones or smartwatches). The payment terminal accepts the transaction under the assumption that the user authenticated on a mobile device, completing the purchase without PIN entry. The authors demonstrated this live using a 200 Swiss franc transaction.

To remediate the vulnerability, the authors proposed activating the card's SDAD signature by flipping a single bit in one of the terminal's commands. Because this change is implemented on the terminal side, it does not require replacing existing cards in circulation. Other findings, such as attacks against offline low-value transactions that lead terminals to accept charges later rejected by issuing banks, lack authentication and require card reissuance to resolve.

### Takeaways
The findings highlight that human analysis alone cannot manage the branching complexity and state space of critical real-world protocols. Formal protocol verification using tools such as Tamarin should be integrated directly into development and standardization processes to identify and resolve vulnerabilities before mass deployment.

talks.title: Proof-of-Learning: Definitions and Practice
talks.teaser: Explains Proof-of-Learning, a logging-based method for proving how a machine learning model was trained.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses two problems in machine learning. The first is ownership: a publicly hosted model can be copied through model extraction, and an arbitrator then needs a way to tell who really trained it. The second is trust in distributed or outsourced training, where a worker may not perform the delegated computation. Existing defenses have drawbacks. Watermarking and fingerprinting trade away model accuracy and require changes to training, while verifiable computation often forces architecture changes or limits which operations can be used.

The speakers propose Proof-of-Learning, a record of the whole training effort rather than only the final weights. A proof stores the weight sequence, the indices of the data used, and auxiliary information such as the learning rate, with full weights saved every k steps. Verification first uses a KS test to check that the starting weights look freshly initialized, then replays training step by step from each checkpoint, so only one step's randomness has to match. Because checking only the largest updates is cheaper, the team examined spoofing. An adversary who splices a stolen model into an otherwise valid proof leaves a large gap that gets caught. Tracing weights backward with inverse gradient updates produced verification errors around ten times larger, so that approach also fails.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support these results. Since the method mostly adds logging to an existing training loop, it leaves model utility essentially unchanged. The main limitations are the cost of verification, which approaches retraining when checkpoints are frequent, and the storage needed for proofs. Nondeterminism from hardware and libraries is the largest source of verification error, so reducing that noise and cutting verification cost are named as next steps.

talks.title: They Would do Better if They Worked Together: The Case of Interaction Problems Between Password ...
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning They Would do Better if They Worked Together: The Case of Interaction Problems Between Password ....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Nicolas Swearman discusses research on interaction problems between password managers and websites. While password managers are recommended to alleviate the burden of memorizing unique, randomly generated credentials, their real-world operation relies heavily on browser extensions that inspect web pages and inject authentication functionality. Due to the complexity of website architectures and varying implementations of login and registration forms, password managers frequently fail to detect fields or properly autofill credentials.

### Key Topics
- **Password Reuse and User Perceptions**: According to a February 2019 online survey, 69% of participants believed they were very good at protecting online accounts and 59% believed they were safer than average. However, 52% admitted to reusing passwords across multiple accounts, 13% reused passwords for all accounts, and only 24% reported using a password manager.
- **Dataset and Issue Mining**: The researchers collected user-reported bugs across open-source repositories and extension stores, gathering 1,300 reviews across 15 password managers on the Chrome Web Store, 400 GitHub issues, and 729 Chrome Web Store support requests. Three authors filtered these reports for website interaction issues, establishing a codebook that yielded 152 relevant issues.
- **Categorization and Minimal Working Examples**: From the 152 issues, the authors identified 7 broad categories and 39 distinct problematic interaction patterns. They constructed minimal working examples (MWEs)—simplified HTML snippets isolating the specific form or script interaction (e.g., Google's two-page login flow)—to systematically evaluate password manager behavior.
- **Automated Testing Setup**: Testing was performed using an automated Selenium script that launched clean Chrome environments with the target password manager installed, allowing researchers to evaluate compatibility against each minimal working example.

### Technical Details
The authors evaluated the 15 most downloaded password managers on the Chrome Web Store alongside 3 built-in browser vendor managers (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Microsoft Edge). 

Key findings and failure modes include:
- **Failure Rates**: 17 out of the 39 interactions failed to operate seamlessly across more than five password managers. Notably, no single password manager succeeded across all tested interactions.
- **Domain Matching**: Password managers struggle to safely decide whether credentials should be shared across subdomains or related domains without risking credential leakage.
- **Input Field Attributes**: Lack of standardized support or handling for attributes like `autocomplete` or length constraints (e.g., maximum password length).
- **JavaScript Interferences**: Client-side scripts that intercept inputs (such as scripts that capture keystrokes and replace field values with asterisks prior to form submission) or dynamically generated input fields that appear only after explicit user interaction.
- **Complex Form Elements**: Multi-input PIN fields composed of separate HTML tags, split name fields (first name and last name instead of a single username), and pages containing multiple forms simultaneously (such as registration and login forms on one page).

### Takeaways and Proposed Solutions
- **Adoption of Existing Standards**: Many compatibility issues can be resolved immediately if web developers and password managers consistently support existing HTML standards, particularly the `autocomplete` attribute (including support for one-time passcodes / TOTP) and input format specifiers.
- **Emerging Specifications**: Adoption of newer standards, such as Apple's proposed `passwordrules` attribute, can allow websites to explicitly communicate password complexity and character requirements directly to password managers.
- **Credential Sharing Standard**: To address domain matching across subdomains (e.g., `example.com` and `auth.example.com`), the authors propose establishing a new HTTP header or HTML tag mechanism (similar to CSP or CORS). Password managers could issue a lightweight HEAD request to verify whether credential sharing is authorized between origins.
- **Replication Package**: The authors released a replication package containing the minimal working example test site, Selenium scripts, and video recordings demonstrating each tested interaction.

talks.title: CryptGPU: Fast Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning on the GPU
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding CryptGPU: Fast Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning on the GPU.
talks.summary:
### Overview
CryptGPU is an end-to-end framework enabling privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) inference and training directly on GPUs. As machine learning models scale from small networks (like LeNet on MNIST) to deeper architectures (such as ResNet and VGG-16 on ImageNet), the primary performance bottleneck shifts from secure multi-party computation (MPC) communication overhead to raw computation, with linear layers accounting for up to 98% of training time in prior work. To bridge the massive performance gap between plain text and private machine learning—which historically reached 23,000x for inference (CryptFlow) and 42,000x for training (Falcon)—CryptGPU keeps all computations on the GPU, yielding substantial speedups across both linear and non-linear layers.

### Key Topics
- **Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML):** Addressing data privacy challenges in collaborative healthcare and diagnostic scenarios where patient data and proprietary model weights must remain confidential during inference and training.
- **Threat Model & Security Assumptions:** Operating under a three-party computation (3PC) framework with semi-honest security and an honest majority, permitting at most one semi-honest corrupt party who follows protocol execution but attempts to learn additional information.
- **Bridging MPC Fixed-Point Arithmetic and GPU CUDA Kernels:** Overcoming the lack of native CUDA kernels for 32-bit or 64-bit integer fixed-point arithmetic by embedding integer operations into floating-point hardware.
- **GPU-Friendly MPC Protocols:** Designing parallel, branch-free non-linear operations (such as approximation-based division and limit-based exponentiation) to maximize GPU parallel execution rather than relying on control-flow-heavy approaches like garbled circuits.

### Technical Details
CryptGPU is built on top of PyTorch and CrypTen, structuring its architecture around three primary pillars:
1. **Replicated Secret Sharing:** Utilizing 3-party replicated additive secret sharing as the core primitive, where each party holds two out of three shares, efficiently supporting addition and multiplication.
2. **Embedding Fixed-Point Arithmetic in Floating-Point Computations:** Standard MPC fixed-point representations require 32-bit or 64-bit integer operations, but standard GPU CUDA acceleration is built around floating-point formats. CryptGPU exploits the fact that 64-bit double-precision floats have 52 bits of precision, enabling exact integer representations between -2^52 and 2^52. Using bilinearity, large integers (32-bit or 64-bit) are decomposed into sums of products of smaller 16-bit integers (e.g., (a1 + a2)(b1 + b2)), ensuring intermediate products never exceed 52 bits and execute without precision loss. This functionality is exposed as a reusable `CudaLongTensor` abstraction.
3. **GPU-Friendly Non-Linear Protocols:** Recognizing that GPUs struggle with conditional branching, CryptGPU replaces branch-heavy garbled circuits with approximation-based methods for private division, and uses limit-based approximations to turn exponentiation into sequences of parallel multiplications.

Empirical evaluations indicate that while CryptGPU shows little benefit on small workloads where communication dominates, it significantly outperforms prior state of the art on larger workloads:
- **Inference:** Delivers a 2.5x to 3.7x improvement over Falcon and CryptFlow on networks such as ResNet and VGG-16 on Tiny ImageNet.
- **Training:** Outperforms Falcon by 7x on small models and up to 36x on large models (e.g., AlexNet on Tiny ImageNet).
- **Microbenchmarks:** Microbenchmark tests reveal that running private convolution on GPU is 100x faster than on CPU, and private ReLU is 10x faster.

### Takeaways
CryptGPU demonstrates that GPU acceleration is critical for practical privacy-preserving machine learning at scale, effectively mitigating the severe computation bottlenecks in linear layer evaluation. While the current system is limited to single-GPU computation, future work includes expanding to multi-GPU clusters and designing dedicated MPC protocols optimized specifically around GPU parallel capabilities.

talks.title: Fingerprinting the Fingerprinters: Learning to Detect Browser Fingerprinting Behaviors
talks.teaser: Shows how combining script syntax and runtime behavior lets a machine learning detector find browser fingerprinting scripts.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the move from cookies to browser fingerprinting, where trackers combine values exposed by JavaScript APIs and HTTP headers, such as screen size, fonts and plugins, into an identifier that is hard to remove. It explains why current defenses fall short: browsers restrict or randomize APIs, which can break legitimate sites, while earlier heuristic detectors are narrow and only inspect execution traces, so they miss obfuscated or event-triggered scripts.

The speaker presents FP-Inspector, which models each script in two ways. A syntactic view turns the source into an abstract syntax tree that normalizes coding style and captures API usage in context, such as repeated text measurement in canvas fingerprinting. A semantic view instruments Firefox to record API call frequency and generalized arguments during execution. Both views train decision-tree ensemble classifiers, relabeled over several rounds because the heuristic labels used as ground truth are only partly correct. Reported results include about 99% accuracy, 26% more detected scripts than the heuristics, and a 10% accuracy gain from combining both views.

Applying the detector to the web, the speaker finds that nearly a third of the top 1,000 sites deploy fingerprinting, with deployment growing since a 2016 study and concentrated on ad-supported and news sites. The most prevalent vendors also offer cross-site tracking or anti-ad-fraud services. The implementation and detections are open source, and filter lists such as EasyPrivacy have adopted them, with EasyPrivacy adding a dedicated fingerprinting category.

talks.title: Method Confusion Attack on the Bluetooth Pairing Process
talks.teaser: Shows how a design flaw in Bluetooth pairing lets an attacker force devices into mismatched pairing methods and intercept traffic.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Maximilian from churchnets presents a critical vulnerability in Bluetooth pairing protocols called a method confusion attack. As Bluetooth has become the standard for ad hoc device pairing (over 4 billion devices shipped annually as of 2019), it supports numerous device types with varying capabilities and security needs. However, the protocol's complexity to accommodate diverse device classes introduces a fundamental design flaw.

## Key Technical Problem

Bluetooth's pairing process begins with unencrypted interface negotiation, where devices exchange their capabilities and select an appropriate pairing method before establishing secure communication. An attacker can manipulate this negotiation to force two devices into different pairing methods while each believes both are using the same method.

## Pairing Methods Analyzed

Two primary methods are vulnerable:
- **Numeric comparison**: Devices exchange public key material and generate 6-digit decimal hash values displayed on screens. Users visually confirm the values match, authenticating the key material.
- **Pass key entry**: One device generates a random 6-digit value the user transfers to another device, creating a shared secret for secure key exchange.

The critical flaw: numeric comparison values are inherently public (derived from publicly exchanged cryptographic data), while pass key values must remain completely confidential. Both methods exchange indistinguishable 6-digit decimal values.

## Attack Mechanism

The attacker performs pass key entry with device A (prompting the user to input a value) and numeric comparison with device B (displaying the fingerprint). The attacker captures the numeric comparison fingerprint from device B and feeds it into device A as the confidential pass key. This violates pass key entry's security assumption that the value remains confidential, allowing the attacker to complete the zero-knowledge secret key exchange with both devices separately and establish a man-in-the-middle position.

## User Study Results

Researchers conducted a user study where participants performed pairings while the method confusion attack ran silently in the background. No participants detected the attack, even when shown different vendor dialogues, indicating users cannot reliably identify which pairing method is active.

## Mitigation and Future Direction

Current temporary fix: user warnings and clearer UI indication of the pairing method. However, this cannot prevent the attack. The researchers are developing tools to analyze protocols for such flaws and creating a new protocol that supports multiple pairing methods while being formally verifiable to exclude such design vulnerabilities.

talks.teaser: Shows how modest changes to KVM let its core be formally verified for VM confidentiality and integrity.
talks.summary: Xiwei Lee presents microverification, a strategy to prove confidentiality and integrity properties of commodity KVM without replacing its feature set. SCKVM splits Linux-hosted KVM into a verified K-core hypervisor mode component and an untrusted K-serve kernel that keeps familiar virtualization services. On ARM, K-core controls stage-two nested page tables, identity maps service memory, traps faults, and isolates VM CPU state while K-serve allocates pages. Verification uses layered refinement with security-preserving traces so concurrent page-table updates cannot smuggle cross-VM mappings during multiprocessor races. The checked core is roughly four thousand lines plus a verified crypto helper, with about six thousand lines of Coq proofs. Benchmarks on server-class hardware report modest overhead versus stock KVM while retaining multiprocessor VMs, device passthrough paths, and workloads such as Apache, Memcached, and MySQL.

talks.title: Compact Certificates of Collective Knowledge
talks.teaser: Introduces a compact certificate scheme that lets many weighted parties prove agreement on a fact with small, fast-to-check proofs.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem: many parties, such as computers watching the same attack source, people seeing a rare event, or nodes in a blockchain tracking its state, want a short way to prove that a majority agrees on a fact. Bundling one signature per party works in principle, but the certificate grows with the number of parties and becomes expensive to check. The speaker presents a cryptographic primitive called a compact certificate scheme, designed to handle parties with different weights, faulty or malicious participants, and a verifier that does not need to trust the prover.

The construction commits to all signatures in a Merkle tree whose leaves also hold the start of each signer's weight range. The verifier keeps only a short commitment to the public keys and weights, and it sends random challenges sampled in proportion to weight. The prover opens the matching leaves. A prover who overstates the total signed weight must commit to some leaf that fails for at least one challenge, so enough queries expose the cheat. More signed weight means fewer queries are needed and smaller certificates. The scheme is made non-interactive with the Fiat-Shamir heuristic and is shown to be a random-oracle proof of knowledge, with certificate size polylogarithmic in the number of parties.

The implementation is about 1,200 lines of Go, using Ed25519 signatures and truncated SHA-512. At one million parties with 128-bit security, certificates range from under 100 KB to about 900 KB, compared with 11 to 77 MB for the naive approach, which makes them 50 to 280 times smaller. Verification takes roughly 10 to 80 ms, 300 to 4,000 times faster than the naive method at that scale. Generation stays under 60 seconds on a single thread and is at most twice the baseline cost. The speaker notes that the paper also covers use in blockchains with stake-weighted voting.

talks.title: Red Belly: a Deterministic Scalable Open Permissioned Blockchain
talks.teaser: Presents a leaderless, deterministic blockchain design that scales throughput through superblocks and sharded signature verification.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Red Belly, a blockchain designed around three goals: security under Byzantine failures with optimal resilience, fairness so that a correct user's transactions are committed even when a malicious user floods the system, and scalability that grows with the number of machines. It frames an "open" model in which any node can submit signed transactions, while block decisions are restricted to a set of temporarily permitted nodes.

The first technique removes the leader. Every replica proposes directly through a democratic BFT consensus, and transactions are ordered by their age in the mempool so the oldest are proposed first. To scale block decisions, the speaker proposes Set Byzantine Consensus, where the decided output is a non-conflicting union of the proposed sets, combined into one superblock. More participating nodes therefore mean more blocks decided per instance. The second technique shards signature verification: each transaction is checked by a subset of nodes, and f+1 matching answers establish validity, with extra checks when responses disagree.

The evaluation on AWS with 20 to 300 machines showed throughput rising with system size, with a peak near 660,000 transactions per second around 300 nodes, even though latency roughly doubled. Tests on geographically spread virtual machines found it outperforming a PBFT-based system, while HoneyBadger BFT runs became too slow beyond about 100 nodes. A 1000-VM deployment across four continents reported an average latency of about 3 seconds. The practical takeaway is that leaderless consensus, superblocks and verification sharding can let an open permissioned-style chain scale.

talks.title: Cross-Domain Access Control Encryption -- Arbitrary-policy, Constant-size, Efficient
talks.teaser: Presents a practical cross-domain access control encryption scheme with constant-size ciphertexts for arbitrary policies.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces cross-domain access control encryption, a variant where a central authority issues encryption keys and a separate receiver authority issues decryption keys. It targets malicious writers who might leak secrets through their own outgoing traffic, so cryptography enforces which senders can reach which receivers. A sanitizer rewrites ciphertexts in transit while remaining honest but curious.

Earlier constructions either replicated single-user schemes, which needs exponentially many copies for arbitrary policies, or relied on heavyweight functional encryption for general circuits. The proposed scheme represents the recipient set as one group element, called an aggregator, and combines structure-preserving signatures with identity-based broadcast encryption. Senders prepare a sanitization-ready ciphertext with proofs of well-formedness, so the sanitizer can work without any key and the ciphertext size stays constant. The cost is that encryption needs all other recipients, so a recipient can infer the central authority, a weaker anonymity notion the speaker considers sufficient.

The prototype uses a 462-bit BN curve without preprocessing. Setup, encryption key generation and decryption helper runtime grows linearly with the number of receivers, while other steps stay constant, and all run in seconds even for a thousand receivers. Security is selective, matching prior work, with adaptive security left open. The speaker closes by flagging post-quantum constructions as a remaining open problem.

Nadia Bartol discusses BCG consultants’ remote collaboration, home-network guidance, and a deflected colleague-security survey. Dr. Gail Pomper explains Dreamport’s unclassified outreach, CMMC education going virtual, and integrating security into acquisition tiers. The panel closes on board-level cyber risk, IT–OT culture gaps, SDL practices, and certification frameworks like CMMC and IEC 62443.

talks.title: Throwing Darts in the Dark? Detecting Bots with Limited Data using Neural Data Augmentation
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Throwing Darts in the Dark? Detecting Bots with Limited Data using Neural Data Augmentation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Steve on behalf of a research collaboration between the University of Illinois, Virginia Tech, and Shape Security, this talk focuses on developing machine learning (ML) models for cybersecurity when labeled data is scarce. Using bot detection as a primary case study—covering threats like account takeover and web scraping—the presentation addresses three major challenges: the scarcity of ground-truth labels, concept drift caused by evolving attacker behavior, and the poor generalizability of highly customized domain features across different web services.

### Key Topics
- **Hybrid Bot Detection Strategy:** The architecture prioritizes rule-based detection for high-precision, low-cost coverage of common bots, deploying machine learning specifically to catch advanced bots that evade static rules by mutating their behavior.
- **Frequency-Based Feature Encoding:** Replacing raw application-specific features with generic network features (e.g., URL, cookie, browser), converted dynamically into frequency distributions using cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) over a sliding window.
- **Neural Data Augmentation:** A specialized dual-generator Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture tailored for security contexts where benign data is representative, but malicious data is scarce, biased, and rapidly shifting.

### Technical Details
- **Dataset & Ground Truth:** The research evaluated 23 million network requests collected across three distinct websites (A, B, and C) spanning three months of data over a one-year period. Ground-truth labels were primarily established via user CAPTCHA interactions.
- **Feature Processing:** To avoid raw string dependencies and generalize across services, features are encoded based on frequency percentiles in an empirical CDF. A daily sliding window updates the distribution dynamically to handle unseen items and concept drift in real time.
- **Data Synthesis Architecture:** Standard GANs merely mimic existing samples, which fails against adapting bots. The proposed method splits malicious samples into clusters and outliers using DBSCAN:
  1. *Cluster Data Synthesis:* Synthesizes data near existing bot clusters by expanding boundaries cautiously, becoming less aggressive near benign data regions.
  2. *Outlier Data Synthesis:* Aggressively synthesizes data outward in the complementary space outside benign regions to anticipate future bot variants.
  3. *Discriminator Role:* Functions as the downstream classifier trained to differentiate benign users from both real and synthetic malicious bots.

### Takeaways
- **Rule and ML Complementarity:** Rule-based detection captured roughly 80% of bots, while adding the ML pipeline boosted detection to over 90%.
- **Robustness Under Extreme Label Scarcity:** When trained on just 1% of labeled data, the proposed method achieved F1 scores comparable to an LSTM trained on 100% of labeled data across evaluated services.
- **Mitigating Long-Term Model Decay:** Evaluating a model trained in August 2018 on data from January and September 2019 demonstrated that periodic model retraining with only 1% of new data per month effectively restores detection performance.

talks.title: Krace: Data Race Fuzzing for Kernel File Systems
talks.teaser: Introduces a fuzzer that tracks cross-thread interleavings alongside code coverage to find data races in Linux kernel file systems.
talks.summary:
Data races happen when threads access the same memory location without locking or ordering, and at least one of those accesses is a write. The talk argues that the Linux kernel, and file systems such as Btrfs with many concurrent background threads, is a likely place for such bugs. Conventional kernel fuzzers rely on code coverage and usually notice only memory errors that crash the kernel. Data races often return a wrong error code without crashing anything, so a separate race checker is needed to flag them.

The talk presents Krace, which adds a second coverage dimension to fuzzing. Edge coverage alone cannot distinguish runs that hit the same branches in different thread orders. Tracking every instruction-level ordering is infeasible, so the tool records only cross-thread write-to-read pairs on shared addresses, which fit in a small bitmap. An interleaving generator injects delays before shared memory accesses to shift which thread defines a value another thread reads. Seeds that reach new bits are kept for further mutation. On Btrfs, concurrency coverage sometimes kept growing after edge coverage leveled off, and the approach also reached slightly more edge coverage than the baseline fuzzer.

Across Btrfs, ext4 and the virtual file system layer, the authors reported 23 bugs, at least 11 of which were confirmed as harmful. The effects included information loss, violated invariants, kernel crashes and performance degradation. The main takeaway is that for highly concurrent code, coverage should capture thread interactions as well as control flow. Future work includes structured input generation, seed selection and applying the approach to other applications.

talks.title: RAMBleed: Reading Bits in Memory without Accessing Them
talks.teaser: Shows how Rowhammer bit flips can leak RSA key bits from OpenSSH across security domains, even on ECC memory.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces RAMBleed, a technique that lets an unprivileged process read bits stored in memory it has no permission to access. Because DRAM places cells from different security domains next to each other, repeatedly activating neighbouring rows can flip bits in a victim row, and the flip pattern depends on the values stored around it. By hammering rows it owns and observing whether a middle bit flips, an attacker can infer the secret bits in the adjacent rows.

To make this practical, the speaker walks through an end-to-end attack on OpenSSH. The attacker uses a Linux allocator technique to exhaust small blocks until it obtains physically contiguous memory with a known DRAM layout, then applies a frame feng shui method to steer the server's RSA signing key into chosen frames by opening TCP connections to the daemon. In the demonstration, the attack recovered about 68% of a 2048-bit RSA key at roughly 0.3 bits per second with 82% accuracy. A probabilistic key-recovery algorithm then reconstructed the full key within a couple of hours.

The talk closes with ECC memory. ECC corrects flipped bits, but the correction path causes large read latency spikes that an attacker can time to detect a flip, so ECC slows the attack without stopping it. The takeaway is that Rowhammer threatens confidentiality as well as integrity, and that ECC alone does not prevent cross-domain data leakage.

talks.title: Plundervolt: Software-Based Fault Injection Attacks against Intel SGX
talks.teaser: Shows how undervolting Intel CPUs via an undocumented MSR induces faults that break SGX integrity and recover RSA and AES keys.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether software running with root privileges can induce hardware faults in Intel CPUs and whether those faults can defeat Intel SGX, the trusted execution environment meant to protect enclave code even from a root attacker. The speaker explains dynamic voltage and frequency scaling and identifies an undocumented model-specific register, 0x150, that allows voltage to be lowered from software.

By undervolting close to the crash point, the research produced repeatable multiplication errors, first as a single flipped bit and later as contiguous flips. Stability was best at mid-range frequencies such as 1 GHz. The same faults appeared while code ran inside an enclave, and identical bit positions showed up across machines and processor generations from Skylake onward. One faulty RSA decryption inside SGX, combined with the Lenstra attack against the Chinese remainder theorem optimisation, exposed a prime factor of the private key. Separately, a fault during AES-NI rounds allowed differential fault analysis to recover an AES key, and a fault in pointer arithmetic caused enclave data to be written to untrusted memory.

The speaker reports responsible disclosure to Intel, which placed the findings under embargo and mentioned other groups working on related attacks. The main takeaway is that the CPU is pushed outside its specification, which differs from the speculative-execution issue LVI, where the processor behaves as designed. Practitioners should see that trusted execution does not automatically shield enclaves from voltage and frequency manipulation by privileged software.

talks.title: ZEXE: Enabling Decentralized Private Computation
talks.teaser: Presents a system for private offline computation, with transactions that hide their program and verify in near-constant time.
talks.summary:
Public ledgers such as Ethereum, Tezos and EOS verify transactions by re-execution, so every node repeats every computation. This caps throughput at the weakest node and permanently exposes the program run, its inputs and its caller. Zexe, which stands for zero-knowledge execution, lets users compute offline and publish a proof of correctness instead. The transaction reveals none of the program, inputs or invoker, and checking it takes time independent of the underlying computation, with transactions under a kilobyte and verification under 50 milliseconds.

The talk starts from Zerocash, which hides senders, receivers and values through serial-number double-spend checks and a zero-knowledge proof covering membership, correct construction and value conservation. Generalising this to arbitrary data with one predicate per record allows value to appear from nothing, because a record's birth is never checked. Giving each record separate constraints for its creation and its consumption closes that gap. Since universal circuits are roughly 20 times slower, the implementation instead uses proof recursion, where the transaction verifies a proof that a predicate is satisfied.

Efficient recursion needs small circuits that verify SNARK proofs, which requires pairing-friendly elliptic curves. The team presents a way to sample recursion-friendly BLS12 curves, a new curve CP6 built with the Cox-Zimmerman method to verify BLS12-377 proofs, and Edwards curves that make Pedersen hashes and commitments efficient on both. All curves are implemented in a Rust library. The talk closes by pointing to the paper, which applies the model to private user-defined assets, stablecoins and decentralized exchanges.

talks.title: An Analysis of Pre-installed Android Software
talks.teaser: Measures pre-installed Android apps across hundreds of vendors, exposing unverifiable certificates, hidden permissions and privacy risks.
talks.summary:
Android phones often ship with extra system apps added by chipset makers, phone vendors, carriers and their partners. These apps sit on the read-only system partition, can run in the background, and usually cannot be removed without rooting the device. Because such apps are rarely published, the team built a freely available scanner app that, with user consent, collected pre-installed apps from devices. This gathered about 82,000 unique apps from more than 200 vendors.

The developers were mapped through signing certificates, but these are self-signed and cannot be checked against a trusted root, so a claimed owner means little. The team found over 90 certificates claiming to be from Google, and many apps whose company could not be identified. Advertising, analytics and social network libraries appeared in thousands of apps without user consent. Nearly 5,000 custom permissions were found, mostly undocumented, with about 10 percent not attributable to any company. Heat maps revealed partnerships, such as Facebook permissions spread across major vendors. Static analysis showed many apps could read sensitive data such as the IMEI, and some known malware families and rooting tools were present. Dynamic analysis was not run, so actual data leaks remain unconfirmed.

The speaker urged better documentation of custom permissions, published certificate hashes so fake signatures can be spotted, and tighter Google control over what gets preinstalled. Regulators also have a role to play. Part of the dataset is made available to the research community.

talks.title: Enabling Rack-scale Confidential Computing Using Heterogeneous Trusted Execution Environment
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Enabling Rack-scale Confidential Computing Using Heterogeneous Trusted Execution Environment.
talks.summary:
Zhu Jianping presents HETD, a heterogeneous trusted execution environment designed to enable rack-scale confidential computing in data centers without chip-level modifications. The motivation addresses the need to protect pooled computing resources (CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs) commonly distributed across modern data centers, where existing TEE solutions either require hardware changes or cannot efficiently support such architectures.

The HETD system architecture consists of a sealed chassis containing a security controller (SSC based on MCPU and FPGA), PCI Express fabric for resource management, multiple proxy microservice nodes with accelerators, and untrusted external server nodes. The design separates security functions (in SSC) from computation (in HETD enclaves running standard software like TensorFlow and GPU drivers), minimizing the trusted computing base.

Key technical components include elastic resource allocation via PCIe fabric's software-defined and flexible topology properties, secure enclave lifecycle management through secure reboot procedures that clear memory and reset accelerators, and data protection using AES-GCM encryption with separate message queues for ciphertext and plaintext areas. An FPGA-based cryptographic controller enforces isolation, with no direct shared space between components. Trust establishment uses a two-layer public key design (endorsement key and attestation key) with remote attestation and symmetric key negotiation.

The threat model considers a strong adversary controlling the software stack and capable of side-channel attacks via network traffic analysis. Physical snooping on the host memory bus is in scope but not within the sealed HETD box. Covert channels, attacks on cryptographic algorithms, and denial-of-service attacks are out of scope.

The prototype integrates two Xilinx PX 9797 boards, one SC node, four processor nodes, and four NVIDIA GPUs. Performance evaluation shows throughput overhead under 5% for most workloads, with batch-size-dependent latency overhead reaching 42.96% for inference and 18.54% for training at batch size 8. Encryption overhead is small and stable. Multiple-GPU scalability matches the baseline, demonstrating that elastic resource allocation can improve single-enclave performance without sacrificing horizontal scalability.

The system provides four security guarantees in a Platform-as-a-Service model: isolation from other enclaves on the same proxy node, isolation from past and future users, protection from untrusted hosts, and protection from cloud providers. The design resists side-bleed attacks on sealed FPGAs and cold boot attacks when unauthorized chassis opening takes longer than power-removal-based memory extraction.

talks.title: Flaw Label: Exploiting IPv6 Flow Label
talks.teaser: Shows how IPv6 flow label values leak a static per-device key that enables cross-browser tracking on Windows, Linux and Android.
talks.summary:
IPv6 adoption is growing, and modern operating systems prefer IPv6 when a server offers it, so many users send IPv6 traffic without knowing it. Since Windows 10 1703 and Linux 4.3, the 20-bit flow label field is filled with generated values rather than zeros. The researchers reverse engineered how each platform builds it. On Windows, the label comes from a Toeplitz hash of the addresses and ports, keyed by a 320-bit value that changes only at reboot. On Linux and Android, UDP labels come from a Jenkins hash keyed by a static 32-bit value, also set only at boot.

Because that key persists across browsers, network changes and temporary address rotation, it can act as a device identifier. The Toeplitz hash is bilinear, so an attacker who controls the destination fields can XOR inputs to isolate key bits, recovering more than 80 bits from a few crafted UDP packets or nine TCP packets. The generic case reduces to linear equations. For Linux and Android, the 32-bit key can simply be enumerated. An HTML snippet on any third-party page can trigger the needed traffic through WebRTC. A passive observer, such as a server or a man-in-the-middle, can derive the same identifier from ordinary IPv6 traffic and link past activity to a device. The attacks worked across 19 networks, including VPNs.

Windows 10 versions 1703 through 1903 were affected and fixed in the November 2019 update. Linux kernels 4.3 through 5.3.9 were affected and moved to a keyed hash with a 128-bit key. The authors argue that vendors should use strong cryptographic functions with adequate key sizes whenever attacker-observable values feed into identifiers.

talks.title: IJON: Exploring Deep State Spaces via Fuzzing
talks.teaser: Explains how annotations that add selective value feedback help fuzzers escape large equivalence classes and reach deeper program states.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Academic research on fuzzing predominantly focuses on fully automated approaches such as AFL and libFuzzer. While automation simplifies testing across diverse security scenarios, security practitioners often require finer control over fuzzer behavior. IJON (presented phonetically as Ejon) introduces an approach where human experts guide fuzzers using lightweight annotations. By combining standard code coverage feedback with selective value feedback on specific data points within the program's state space, IJON enables fuzzers to explore deep state spaces without becoming overwhelmed by state noise.

### Key Topics
- **Equivalence Classes and Feedback Limitations**: Modern fuzzers divide the input space into equivalence classes based on code coverage, discarding mutations that produce no new coverage. When equivalence classes are too vast—such as in complex state machines or arithmetic constraints—mutations fail to reach interesting states.
- **Selective Value Feedback**: Instead of tracking all program state (which causes noise and state explosion) or relying purely on code coverage, analysts add inline annotations to direct the fuzzer toward specific values or exploration goals.
- **Feedback Primitives**: IJON introduces feedback primitives such as state-tracking annotations and optimization feedback (e.g., maximizing coordinates or loop counters, minimizing arithmetic differences).
- **Limitations in Interactive Applications**: Long-running or interactive inputs face a severe cubic disadvantage: input queues expand, promising inputs become longer (leading to fewer mutations on critical bytes), and individual executions slow down drastically.

### Technical Details
- **Maze Solving**: In a modified maze game allowing revisiting of board positions, standard fuzzers and KLEE fail because code coverage is exhausted after pressing W, S, A, and D once. A one-line IJON annotation directing the fuzzer to treat new (X, Y) coordinate combinations as new coverage enabled AFL to solve the maze in seconds.
- **Protocol and Format Parsing (libpng)**: In stateful parsing (like FTP or chunk-based formats like PNG), identical code executes repeatedly across states. In `libpng`, tracking the last four observed chunk headers created artificial coverage that allowed AFL to discover a bug requiring a specific sequence of chunks without needing a full file format specification.
- **Maximization and Optimization**: In an integer factorization example, minimizing the difference between equation sides guided the fuzzer toward solutions. Applied to Super Mario Bros., maximizing the player's X coordinate turned AFL into an effective speed-running bot.
- **Vulnerability Discovery & CGC Evaluation**: An inline annotation targeting a `malloc` call quickly confirmed an integer overflow resulting in a zero-sized allocation. Evaluating undefeated DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge (CGC) binaries (via Trail of Bits' x86 port), IJON solved a third of inspected challenges by removing checksum checks during fuzzing and using AFL crash exploration mode with maximization annotations—replicating T-Fuzz results without symbolic execution. Other solved cases involved maximizing loop counters, single pointers, or bypassing string comparisons.

### Takeaways
IJON demonstrates that minimal, human-in-the-loop annotations can bridge the gap where fully automated coverage-guided fuzzers fail. It also highlights open challenges for automated fuzzing, including long-running interactive targets, loop counters, and deep checksum logic.

talks.title: Transparent Polynomial Delegation and Its Applications to Zero Knowledge Proof
talks.teaser: Presents a transparent polynomial delegation scheme that enables fast, post-quantum zero-knowledge proofs without trusted setup.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with zero-knowledge proofs, where a prover convinces a verifier that a computation on a secret input gives a claimed output without revealing that input. Completeness, soundness and zero knowledge are the core guarantees, and proof generation time, proof size and verification time are the main efficiency measures. The speaker points to Zcash, which validates transactions on a public blockchain while keeping addresses and amounts hidden. Its zk-SNARK, however, needs a function-specific trusted setup, has slow proving, and its security depends on discarding a secret generated by a trusted party.

The talk then turns to interactive proofs based on the GKR protocol, which have fast proving but were made zero-knowledge only through polynomial commitments that required a trusted setup or were not post-quantum secure. The speaker's work builds a transparent zero-knowledge polynomial delegation scheme. It removes the trusted setup, relies only on symmetric-key primitives, and is a candidate for post-quantum security. The key idea is to have the prover handle the computation of the evaluation vector for the inverse and forward transforms through a small GKR circuit, so the verifier avoids doing that work directly. The prover runs in near-linear time, while verification time and proof size are polylogarithmic.

In experiments, the new scheme's prover was about 8 to 10 times faster than the commitment scheme used in Libra, taking about 12 seconds for a polynomial of size 2^20, though its proofs are larger. Plugging it into Libra yields Virgo, a transparent zero-knowledge proof system. For a Merkle tree with 256 leaves hashed with SHA-256, Virgo generated a proof in about 53 seconds and verified it in about 15 milliseconds. The speaker also notes the scheme could support verifiable secret sharing with active security. The takeaway is that transparent, post-quantum-friendly proofs with fast proving are feasible, at the cost of larger proof sizes.

talks.title: SPECTECTOR: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows
talks.teaser: Presents a semantic notion of speculative non-interference and a symbolic tool that flags Spectre v1 leaks in compiled code.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how to tell whether a program stays secure when it runs on a CPU that uses speculative execution, with branch prediction as the running example. It recaps how mispredicted work is rolled back at the architectural level while cache changes persist, which is the basis of Spectre variant 1. The speaker proposes speculative non-interference, a semantic security property requiring that a program leaks no more under speculative execution than under ordinary in-order execution. The model combines a standard semantics, a speculative semantics parametric in a branch prediction oracle, and an attacker who observes memory addresses, program counter changes and the start and end of speculation.

To find leaks, the approach symbolically executes a program under the speculative semantics with an always-mispredict oracle, producing symbolic traces that pair path conditions with observations. A leak is a pair of states that agree on non-speculative observations but differ on speculative ones. The tool, SPECTECTOR, translates x64 assembly into an intermediate language and uses an SMT solver. In a first case study, 15 Spectre v1 variants were compiled with three compilers under different mitigations and optimization levels, giving 240 programs. Leaks appeared in unprotected builds, a previously reported Microsoft compiler issue was confirmed, and most speculative load hardening builds were proven secure, except two with minor leaks.

A second case study examined scalability on a large real-world codebase. Challenges included obtaining realistic security policies, covering a broad instruction set and handling path explosion, and the trade-offs made to cope with them affected soundness and completeness. Across tens of thousands of traces, checking the property took roughly the same order of time as discovering the symbolic paths, so the approach adds no fundamental bottleneck beyond those of symbolic execution. The tool is available on GitHub.

talks.title: Detection of Electromagnetic Interference Attacks on Sensor Systems
talks.teaser: Presents a method that detects electromagnetic interference attacks on sensor systems by randomly switching the sensor on and off.
talks.summary:
Sensor wires can act as unintended antennas, so an attacker can use electromagnetic interference to inject a signal that changes a sensor's reading, and a microcontroller that trusts that reading has no way to tell. The talk considers this for automotive sensors and nuclear plant temperature monitoring, where a falsified value could drive a harmful decision. Shielding and filtering reduce the injected signal but cannot remove it, so the system must be able to detect attacks itself.

The proposed method switches the sensor off and on in a secret, randomised pattern. The bias voltage is generated by encoding an n-bit secret sequence in Manchester code, and the analog-to-digital converter takes two samples per clock cycle: one while the sensor is powered, expected to be non-zero, and one while it is off, expected to read zero. Without an attack, all non-zero samples match and all zero samples are zero. An attacker who does not know the secret must guess the transition direction in every cycle, so a wrong guess shows up as a mismatched or non-zero sample. The speaker argues that the chance of evading detection over the whole sequence is negligible.

For signals that change too quickly to treat as constant, the method can still flag samples that fall outside the signal's known bandwidth as outliers, so an attacker must alter many samples at once. The practical demonstration uses a thermistor-based temperature sensor in a lab at about 25 degrees. Without detection, an attacker can steer the reading by adjusting the injected power. With detection, a continuous attack is flagged at once, and an attacker who guesses wrong in a single cycle is also caught. The key point is that the sensor can verify its own measurements by switching off at random, provided the secret sequence stays hidden.

talks.title: CrypTFlow : Secure TensorFlow Inference
talks.teaser: Presents a system that compiles TensorFlow inference into secure multi-party computation, scaling to ImageNet-sized networks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a privacy conflict in machine learning inference. A hospital wants to keep its proprietary model secret, and a patient wants to keep their medical data private. Secure multi-party computation can resolve this, but earlier work has struggled with three things: low-level circuit representations that are hard to write and debug, manual conversion from floating-point to fixed-point numbers, and small datasets and models that do not reflect ImageNet-scale networks. Most prior work also assumed honest participants rather than malicious ones.

The speaker presents CrypTFlow, an end-to-end system built from three parts. Ethos is a compiler that takes TensorFlow inference code, generates metadata, and converts floating-point values to fixed-point automatically by sweeping a scale factor and tuning it on a validation set. It then emits semi-honest MPC protocol code through a modular backend, currently ABY and Porthos. Porthos, a three-party protocol for neural network inference, is mentioned but not covered in depth. Aramis turns any semi-honest protocol into a maliciously secure one by having participants run inside Intel SGX and rely only on its integrity guarantee, since confidentiality attacks such as Foreshadow and Plundervolt break the stronger hardware-based approach.

Reported results on ImageNet networks, ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121, run in about 25 seconds in the semi-honest model on a LAN with commodity hardware. Malicious security adds less than 3x overhead, and compilation takes around 40 seconds. For ResNet-50, the chosen scale factor keeps accuracy at the plaintext level. The takeaway is that large, malicious-secure inference is becoming practical, and the authors provide the paper and code.

talks.title: Exploring Adversarial Examples in Malware Detection
talks.teaser: Shows how appended and slack-space byte injections evade neural malware classifiers and what makes them vulnerable.
talks.summary:
Machine learning classifiers that separate malware from benign files increasingly learn directly from raw bytes, avoiding hand-built features. This talk asks whether one shallow convolutional architecture can be evaded by adversarial examples. Naive gradient-based noise breaks executables, so the work focuses on modifications that keep files runnable. Models were trained on a large production dataset and a smaller public one. The speaker showed that a simple attack appending bytes from benign files succeeded far more against the small-dataset model, suggesting that limited training data can produce skewed estimates of attack effectiveness.

A single-step gradient attack that appends perturbation bytes was more effective against the model trained on the larger dataset. The speaker attributed this to the architecture: non-overlapping convolution windows and max pooling without positional information mean appended features cannot be told apart from those at the start of the file. A second method, slack-space FGSM, writes perturbations into the gap between a PE section's raw and virtual sizes, a region not loaded into memory. At the same number of modified bytes it was roughly 40 percent more effective than appending, although the available slack capacity is limited.

The takeaways were that representative training data matters when measuring robustness, that architectural choices such as positional encoding can introduce vulnerability, and that realistic attacker capability requires reasoning about program semantics. Questions raised limits: functionality preservation cannot be fully guaranteed without execution, the approach may depend on the compiler and platform, and simple header-consistency checks could detect such edits.
